title: Saha navavatu: a prayer for us both
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hookLine: a father sends his son back again and again, and a chant for teacher and student
carry: the teacher prays with the student, not above
tomorrow: why say peace three times, and not just once?

cards: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, Varuna, and says: sir, teach me Brahman. Varuna gives him a few pointers and sends him off to find it by tapas, hard inner effort.
Bhrigu comes back: it's food. Seek again by tapas, says his father. Breath.
Understanding. Again. Four times he returns, and four times the answer is the same, patient and unhurried.

teach.b: The same Upanishad gives teacher and student a peace chant to say together before study, known by its first words, saha navavatu.
Tradition chants it with the Katha too, and every peace chant closes the same way: Om, shanti, shanti, shanti. Here's what it asks, in plain words. May it protect us both.
May it nourish us both. May we work together with strength. May our study be full of light.

teach.h: MAY WE NOT TURN AGAINST EACH OTHER.
teach.b: May we not turn against each other. Notice the word both. The teacher doesn't stand outside the prayer, handing it down.

The teacher needs protecting and feeding too. And notice the last request. Of everything that could go wrong in a hard lesson, the chant names this one: that the two people in the room would come to resent each other.
A question pushes, an answer stings, and a little bitterness creeps in.
Many teachers read Varuna as that prayer lived out: four times he sends his son back, and never once sends him away.
This is how Hindu tradition holds learning: guru and student under one prayer, a bond, not a transaction.
So before the text even opens, the chant asks for what the text can't supply: two people still on the same side when the lesson ends.

how: In traditional Upanishad study, teacher and student chant the text's peace chant together before the lesson and again after it, ending with Om shanti shanti shanti.

games.q: your cousin starts sanskrit with a pandit. before the first lesson they chant together, and she asks: why does he pray too, if he already knows it all?
o: it's a formality; only the student really needs the blessing.
the chant is for both: protect us both, and may we not turn against each other.
he's checking her pronunciation before the real lesson starts.
games.why: saha navavatu puts guru and student under one prayer. the teacher asks for protection, strength and no ill will too.

practice: If you chant, say saha navavatu slowly, all the way to the three shantis, holding in mind someone you learn from and someone who learns from you.
If you don't pray, write those two names side by side on one line, and look at them together for the rest of the sit: both under one prayer.

wordCard.voice: The peace chants: lines said before and after the study of an Upanishad, each ending in shanti, peace, three times. Saha navavatu asks for teacher and student both.

orig.note: may it protect us both: the first words of the peace chant teacher and student say together.
